specAnchors.text: explain problems in the disposal of addition polymers, including: their inertness and inability to biodegrade; the production of toxic gases when they are burned

primer.text: From Alkenes you already know how double bonds open up and join monomers into addition polymers with strong carbon-carbon backbones. This note follows those polymers to the end of their useful life, where their greatest strength becomes the planet's problem.

modules.title: Why addition polymers resist breakdown
modules.opening: The same strong carbon-carbon bonds that make addition polymers useful also make them nearly unreactive. Micro-organisms cannot break them down, so buried plastic simply sits there while landfill sites fill up. This lesson explains why inertness is an environmental liability.
keyPoints: Addition polymers are built from many small molecules joined by strong carbon-carbon bonds.
Those strong bonds make the polymers unreactive and chemically inert.
Inert polymers cannot biodegrade, so decomposers cannot break them down.
Landfill disposal takes up valuable land and sites fill up quickly.
The inability to biodegrade is the core disposal problem.

low.restatement: Strong carbon-carbon bonds make addition polymers unreactive and inert. Nothing in the soil can break them down, so landfill sites take up land and fill up fast.
low.analogy: An addition polymer in a landfill is like a stone in a field: the seasons pass, the microbes try, and the stone simply waits.
low.examPointer: Name the property first, inertness, then the consequence, inability to biodegrade; that chain of reasoning earns the marks.

medium.restatement: The strong carbon-carbon backbone makes addition polymers chemically inert, so micro-organisms such as decomposers cannot biodegrade them. Buried waste therefore occupies valuable land and fills sites quickly, which is why disposal is an environmental problem rather than a solved one.
medium.analogy: Their strength is a superpower with a bill: the same armour that survives every product lifetime also survives every refuse tip, indefinitely.
medium.examPointer: Quote both strands for landfill questions: inertness with non-biodegradability, and the space the buried waste consumes.

modules.title: Incineration and its three hazards
modules.opening: Burning looks like a tidy answer, and incineration does release useful heat energy. But the smoke carries costs: carbon dioxide warms the climate, chlorine-bearing plastics release toxic hydrogen chloride, and incomplete burning makes poisonous carbon monoxide. This lesson weighs all three.
keyPoints: Burning polymers releases a lot of heat energy.
It also produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas linked to climate change.
Polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, release toxic hydrogen chloride when burned.
Incomplete combustion during incineration produces carbon monoxide.
Carbon monoxide is toxic because it reduces the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

low.restatement: Burning polymers gives out useful heat but produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Chlorine-bearing plastics give toxic hydrogen chloride, and incomplete burning makes carbon monoxide, which harms the blood.
low.analogy: Incineration is a deal with strings: warmth today, then three separate letters of complaint from the climate, the chlorine and the blood.
low.examPointer: Keep the three hazards separate: dioxide for climate, hydrogen chloride for PVC, monoxide for incomplete burning.

medium.restatement: Incineration recovers a lot of heat energy but emits carbon dioxide, the greenhouse gas driving climate change. Polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, release toxic hydrogen chloride gas, and any incomplete combustion adds carbon monoxide, which lowers the capacity of blood to carry oxygen.
medium.analogy: Think of the flue as a three-lane exit: one lane carries the climate bill, one carries chlorine's poison, and one carries the silent gas that crowds oxygen out of the blood.
medium.examPointer: Match each toxic gas to its trigger: hydrogen chloride needs chlorine in the polymer, monoxide needs incomplete combustion.

glossary.definition: Disposing of waste by burning it; polymers release heat energy but hazardous gases this way.
Chemically unreactive; addition polymers are inert because of their strong carbon-carbon bonds.
To be broken down naturally by micro-organisms; addition polymers are unable to do this.
A site where waste is buried in the ground, filling quickly with non-biodegrading polymers.
Poisonous to living things; hydrogen chloride and carbon monoxide are both toxic gases.

workedExample.prompt: Explain the problems in disposing of addition polymers by a) landfill and b) incineration, naming the gases produced when plastics are burned.
steps: a) Addition polymers are joined by strong C-C bonds, making them unreactive and chemically inert, so they cannot biodegrade — micro-organisms such as decomposers cannot break them down; buried in landfill they take up valuable land and the sites fill quickly.
b) Incineration releases a lot of heat energy, but burning polymers produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.

Polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, release toxic hydrogen chloride when burned, and incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide, which reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Inert and non-biodegradable, so landfill fills with waste. b) Burning gives CO2 (greenhouse gas), HCl from chlorine-containing polymers, and CO from incomplete combustion.
